minor: "Later, in 1944-45, Moscow moved the line west to the river": the source lists the decree as November 1944, with the transfer carried out in early 1945. Either date is defensible, but "November 1944" (or "late 1944") would match the source.

"(quote) Weeks later Russia annexed Crimea, and, in a Russian view, President Putin spoke of Russians divided by borders.": the quote shot does not actually say Putin's words, and "in a Russian view" is awkward. It also implies a link between the treaty and Crimea. Speak the sourced quote aloud and attribute it plainly to Putin on 18 March 2014.
"For generations, families here are said to have had relatives on both banks": no source is listed. It is plausible but unsupported.
"Some commentators in the West asked whether Narva ... could be next": no source is listed for this. The RAND and ICDS sources only partly cover it.
"Border posts at Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa": Koidula and Luhamaa are not on the Narva river, but the line says "the line in use", so it is acceptable.

"In 1944 the Soviet and German front line sat on the river ... Narva was cut in two": the front ran through and around Narva, including a Soviet bridgehead west of the river. This is a simplification, not an error.
"Estonia answers ... children born in Estonia to stateless parents ... get citizenship": in practice the parents apply for it. This is a rounder wording.

"an attack on Narva would be treated as an attack on all of NATO": this is Article 5 wording, but each ally decides its own response. It is better phrased as "NATO's treaty says an attack on one is an attack on all".

shots.vo: Estonia is a country of about 1.4 million people on the Baltic Sea, pressed against Russia's western edge.
Its border with Russia runs about 324 kilometres, mostly down a river and through one huge lake.
The Narva River leaves Lake Peipus and flows 77 kilometres north into the Gulf of Finland.
St Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, lies only about 135 kilometres from Narva in a straight line.
Estonia's own capital, Tallinn, is about 190 kilometres the other way, so Russia's big city is closer.
About 54,000 people live in Narva, which makes it Estonia's third-largest city after Tallinn and Tartu.

shots.vo: It sits in Ida-Viru County, the north-east corner, where most people's first language is Russian.
Across Estonia, about 69 percent of people are ethnic Estonians. In Narva, the figure is about 4.
Census figures show roughly half of Narva holds Estonian citizenship, and about a third holds Russian passports.

On the Estonian bank stands Hermann Castle, begun under Danish rule back in the 1200s.
Facing it, Ivangorod Fortress, built for Moscow's Ivan the Third, has watched this water since 1492.

shots.vo: In the 1400s, Narva was a trading town of the Livonian Order, a German crusader state on the Baltic.
Even then the river was a boundary, between Livonia and the Russian lands of Novgorod on the east bank.
In 1492 Ivan the Third built Ivangorod right opposite, two fortresses face to face.
Russia captured Narva in 1558, and Sweden took it in 1581 and held it for more than a century.
In November 1700, Sweden's young King Charles the Twelfth beat a far larger Russian army outside Narva.
The Swedes attacked in a snowstorm, and the Russian siege lines broke quickly.
shots.prompt: Muted historical map of the Narva River area in November 1700, Narva on the west bank and the Russian siege lines on the east, arrows showing a Swedish attack through falling snow, no signs or lettering on any storefront, screen or package

shots.vo: Yet the line did not move for long: Sweden kept Narva until 1704, when Peter the Great took it, and by 1721 the whole region was Russia's.
Between 1721 and 1918 no international border ran along the river; both banks lay inside the Russian Empire.
Then the empire collapsed. Estonia declared independence in February 1918 and fought for it until 1920.
In the Treaty of Tartu, Soviet Russia recognised Estonia's independence and gave up its claims 'for ever'.

document.title: Peace Treaty of Tartu, 2 February 1920
document.highlight: Russia unreservedly recognises the independence and autonomy of the State of Estonia, and renounces voluntarily and for ever all sovereign rights.

shots.prompt: Duotone plate: a long table with an open treaty, inkwell and pens in a panelled room, winter light; top third dark and plain

shots.vo: The new border ran east of the river, so Ivangorod and its fortress became Estonian too.
In 1940 the Soviet Union occupied Estonia, under a secret pact with Nazi Germany, and the Soviet frontier moved west, so Narva and Ivangorod came under one flag.
In 1944 the Soviet and German front line sat on the river for months and Narva was cut in two.
When the fighting moved on, the old baroque town lay almost entirely in ruins.

shots.vo: Later, in 1944-45, Moscow moved the line west to the river, handing Ivangorod to Soviet Russia.

map.label: NOV 1944 · LINE BACK TO THE RIVER

shots.vo: Estonia also lost the Petseri area further south, about 5 percent of its pre-war land.
After the war, most pre-war residents were not allowed to come back, and the old town was never rebuilt.
Workers came instead from across the Soviet Union, for the rebuilt factories and the giant Kreenholm textile mill.

map.label: NEW WORKERS FROM ACROSS THE USSR

shots.vo: Back then it was only a line between two Soviet republics, and people crossed it without any checks.
In August 1991 Estonia restored its independence, and that inner line suddenly became an international border.
Estonia gave automatic citizenship to citizens from before 1940 and their descendants, restoring its pre-war law.

shots.vo: Most Soviet-era arrivals had to pass a language exam, and many in Narva were left stateless, holding grey 'alien' passports.
In July 1993 Narva held its own vote on autonomy from Tallinn.
About 97 percent said yes, on a turnout of about half.

shots.vo: Estonia's authorities declared that vote invalid, and Narva stayed. But the river line was never formally settled.

map.label: LINE IN USE · NO RATIFIED TREATY

shots.vo: In 2004 Estonia joined NATO and the European Union, and the alliance's edge reached Narva's riverbank.
Estonia and Russia signed a border treaty in 2005, but Russia withdrew after Estonia's parliament added a reference to 1920.
The two sides signed it again in February 2014, but Russia has never ratified it.
Weeks later Russia annexed Crimea, and, in a Russian view, President Putin spoke of Russians divided by borders.

quote.text: The Russian nation became one of the biggest, if not the biggest ethnic group in the world to be divided by borders.

shots.vo: Some commentators in the West asked whether Narva, another Russian-speaking border town, could be next.
Russia's foreign ministry argues that Estonia's language rules and non-citizen status shut many of Narva's people out of politics.
It says Estonia should end both, and that Moscow has a duty to defend Russian speakers abroad.

shots.vo: It points to roughly 60,000 people in Estonia, by Estonia's own count, who still hold no citizenship of any country.

shots.vo: Estonia answers that from 1940 to 1991 Soviet rule pushed its language to the edge, and its laws now protect it.
It adds that since 2016, children born in Estonia to stateless parents who have lived there legally for five years get citizenship.

From 2024, schools began moving to teaching only in Estonian, a switch due to be finished by 2030.

Estonia protested to Moscow. Russia said it disagreed with where the buoys had been placed.

Britain leads a NATO battlegroup at Tapa, about 125 kilometres west of Narva.
Estonia now spends more than 3 percent of its economy on defence, by NATO's 2024 estimate.

shots.vo: It plans about 600 concrete bunkers as part of a Baltic Defence Line announced in 2024.
Beside the Narva bridge, Estonia has also set rows of concrete anti-tank blocks, known as dragon's teeth.
A 2016 RAND wargame found Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Tallinn and Riga in 36 to 60 hours.
So if you lived in Narva, whose promises would you trust? And what could move this map next?
The first path is the quiet one: the river simply stays the line, treaty or no treaty.
Border posts at Narva, Koidula and Luhamaa already check travellers on the line in use, so, analysts say, little would change on the ground.
The second path is pressure without war, such as removed buoys and jammed GPS signals.
In 2024 Finnair paused flights to Tartu for a month after GPS interference, which Estonia blamed on Russia.
On that path, analysts expect the river to be watched even more closely from both banks.
The third path runs through classrooms: by 2030, every school in Narva is due to teach in Estonian.
Supporters say it opens jobs and universities; critics, in Narva and in Moscow, say it pushes a language aside.

shots.vo: And over every path hangs Article 5: an attack on Narva would be treated as an attack on all of NATO.
Which path comes is not decided. But Narva's people have already lived through every version of this border.

shots.vo: Since 1492 the line here has been fortified, erased, moved east, moved back and made international.
That is why many analysts say NATO watches this town, where its edge runs through a story both sides share.
